title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 130 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 611–613 (Night 130, continuing directly from nights-129), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 130 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. Tāj al-Mulūk refuses every other bride and swears he will run wild and kill himself without the lady Dunyā, so his father, King Sulaymān Shāh, sends his vizier with ʿAzīz as guide and rich gifts to the Camphor Islands to ask for her hand, threatening war if her father refuses. The prince spends the night in tears and verse. The envoys are received with honour, but when the request is put, Dunyā flies at the messenger with a stick and swears to kill any husband forced on her, and her father sends the envoys home with her refusal. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْمُوفِيَةُ لِلثَّلٰثِينَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-mūfiyatu li-al-thalāthīna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the completing for the thirty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and thirtieth night,
sentences.n: al-mūfiya li-al-thalāthīn, “the one completing the thirty”: the print names a round-numbered night this way, as it did the hundred and twentieth. It spells thalāthīn without its long alif (ثلثين), its usual spelling; the dagger alif marks the long vowel.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ قَالَ لِضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ إِنَّ وَالِدَ تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ قَالَ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي إِنَّ أَبَاهَا مَلِكٌ وَبِلَادُهُ بَعِيدَةٌ عَنَّا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-wazīra dandāna qāla li-ḍawʾi al-makāni inna wālida tāji al-mulūki qāla lahu yā waladī inna abāhā malikun wa-bilāduhu baʿīdatun ʿannā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the vizier Dandān said to Ḍawʾ al-Makān: (Truly) the father of Tāj al-Mulūk said to him: O my son, her father (is) a king, and his lands (are) far from us;
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the vizier Dandān told Ḍawʾ al-Makān that Tāj al-Mulūk’s father said to him, “My son, her father is a king, and his lands are far from us.
sentences.n: The night opens by repeating the king’s answer to his son, with which the last one ended. inna wālida, “truly the father”: inna after qāla opens the vizier’s words as he spoke them. The print runs al-saʿīd and anna together (السعيدان), as it often does in this formula; the spacing is kept. abāhā, “her father”: the lady Dunyā’s.

sentences.t: فَدَعْ عَنْكَ هَذَا وَادْخُلْ إِلَى قَصْرِ أُمِّكَ فَفِيهِ خَمْسُمِائَةِ جَارِيَةٍ كَالْأَقْمَارِ فَمَنْ أَعْجَبَتْكَ مِنْهُنَّ خُذْهَا وَإِلَّا نَأْخُذُ وَنَخْطُبُ لَكَ بِنْتًامِنْ بَنَاتِ الْمُلُوكِ تَكُونُ أَحْسَنَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-daʿ ʿanka hādhā wa-udkhul ilā qaṣri ummika fa-fīhi khamsumiʾati jāriyatin ka-al-aqmāri fa-man aʿjabatka minhunna khudhhā wa-illā naʾkhudhu wa-nakhṭubu laka bintan min banāti al-mulūki takūnu aḥsana minhā
sentences.l: So leave this from you, and go-in to the palace of your mother, for in it (are) five hundred slave-girls like the moons; so whoever of them pleases you, take her; and if not, we take and ask-in-marriage for you a daughter from the daughters of the kings (who) will be more beautiful than her.
sentences.i: So put this out of your mind, and go into your mother’s palace: there are five hundred slave girls in it, lovely as moons. Whichever of them pleases you, take her; and if none does, we will ask for you the hand of some king’s daughter who will be more beautiful than she is.”
sentences.n: daʿ ʿanka hādhā, “leave this from you”, put it aside. fa-man aʿjabatka minhunna khudhhā, “whoever of them pleases you, take her”: man opens the condition, and the command answers it without fa-. wa-illā, “and if not”. naʾkhudhu wa-nakhṭubu, “we take and ask in marriage”: the two verbs share one object. The print runs bintan and min together (بنتامن); the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ يَا أَبِي لَا أُرِيدُ غَيْرَهَا أَبَدًا وَهِيَ صَاحِبَةُ الْغَزَالِ الَّذِي رَأَيْتُهُ وَلَابُدَّ لِي مِنْهَا وَإِلَّا أَهِجْ فِي الْبَرَارِي وَالْقِفَارِ وَأَقْتُلْ نَفْسِي بِسَبَبِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu yā abī lā urīdu ghayrahā abadan wa-hiya ṣāḥibatu al-ghazāli alladhī raʾaytuhu wa-lā budda lī minhā wa-illā ahij fī al-barārī wa-al-qifāri wa-aqtul nafsī bi-sababihā
sentences.l: So he said to him: O my father, I do not want other-than her ever; and she (is) the owner of the gazelle which I saw; and there-is-no escape for me from her; and if not, I will rage-about in the wildernesses and the wastes and kill myself because of her.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Father, I want no one but her, ever. She is the lady of the gazelle I saw, and I must have her; otherwise I will wander raving through the wilderness and the wastes and kill myself for her sake.”
sentences.n: ṣāḥibat al-ghazāl, “the owner of the gazelle”: the woman who worked the gazelle on the cloth he saw. lā budda lī minhā, “there is no escape for me from her”, I cannot do without her; the print runs lā and budda together (ولابد). wa-illā ahij, “or else I shall run wild”: illā is in lā, “if not”, so the verb that answers it is jussive — ahij, from hāja, yahīju, to rage, to be roused — and wa-aqtul follows it in the same mood. al-barārī wa-al-qifār, “the open lands and the waterless wastes”, a stock pair.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُوهُ أَمْهِلْنِي حَتَّى أُرْسِلَ إِلَى أَبِيهَا وَأَخْطُبَهَا مِنْهُ وَأُبَلِّغَكَ الْمَرَامَ مِثْلَ مَا فَعَلْتُ لِنَفْسِي فِي أُمِّكَ لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ أَنْ يُبَلِّغَكَ الْمَرَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu abūhu amhilnī ḥattā ursila ilā abīhā wa-akhṭubahā minhu wa-uballighaka al-marāma mithla mā faʿaltu li-nafsī fī ummika laʿalla allāha an yuballighaka al-marāma
sentences.l: So his father said to him: Give-me-time until I send to her father and ask-for-her-in-marriage from him and bring-you-to the desire, like what I did for myself in (the matter of) your mother; perhaps God that He bring-you-to the desire.
sentences.i: His father said, “Give me time, until I send to her father and ask him for her hand, and bring you to your desire, just as I did for myself with your mother; perhaps God will grant you your desire.
sentences.n: Sulaymān Shāh won Tāj al-Mulūk’s mother by sending his vizier to ask her father for her, and means to do the same again. ballagha, “to make (someone) reach”: uballighaka al-marām, “I will bring you to what you seek”. laʿalla allāha an yuballighaka, “perhaps God that He bring you”: an after laʿalla is not Classical, but common in this text.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ لَمْ يَرْضَ زَلْزَلْتُ عَلَيْهِ مَمْلَكَتَهُ بِجَيْشٍ آخِرُهُ عِنْدِي وَأَوَّلُهُ عِنْدَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-in lam yarḍa zalzaltu ʿalayhi mamlakatahu bi-jayshin ākhiruhu ʿindī wa-awwaluhu ʿindahu
sentences.l: And if he does not consent, I will make-quake upon him his kingdom with an army whose last (is) with me and whose first (is) with him.
sentences.i: And if he will not consent, I will shake his kingdom down about him with an army whose rear is still here with me while its van is at his door.”
sentences.n: zalzaltu ʿalayhi mamlakatahu, “I will set his kingdom quaking over him”: zalzala is to shake, as an earthquake does; the perfect after in states the threat as good as done. An army whose tail is still at home while its head is at the enemy’s gate is a stock image for a host too long to measure.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَعَا بِالشَّابِّ عَزِيزٍ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي هَلْ أَنْتَ تَعْرِفُ الطَّرِيقَ قَالَ نَعَمْ قَالَ لَهُ أَشْتَهِي مِنْكَ أَنْ تُسَافِرَ مَعَ وَزِيرِي فَقَالَ لَهُ عَزِيزٌ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً يَا مَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma daʿā bi-al-shābbi ʿazīzin wa-qāla lahu yā waladī hal anta taʿrifu al-ṭarīqa qāla naʿam qāla lahu ashtahī minka an tusāfira maʿa wazīrī fa-qāla lahu ʿazīzun samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan yā malika al-zamāni
sentences.l: Then he called for the young-man ʿAzīz and said to him: O my son, do you know the road? He said: Yes. He said to him: I desire of you that you travel with my vizier. So ʿAzīz said to him: Hearing and obedience, O king of the age.
sentences.i: Then he sent for the young man ʿAzīz and said to him, “My son, do you know the way?” “Yes,” he said. “Then I would have you travel with my vizier.” ʿAzīz said to him, “With hearing and obedience, O king of the age.”
sentences.n: daʿā bi-, “called for”: the bi- marks the one summoned. hal anta taʿrifu, “do you know”, with the pronoun set out before the verb, a spoken turn. ashtahī minka an, “I desire of you that”, a courteous command. samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, “(I give) hearing and obedience”, the stock reply to a command.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ أَحْضَرَ وَزِيرَهُ وَقَالَ لَهُ دَبِّرْ لِي رَأْيًا فِي أَمْرِ وَلَدِي يَكُونُ صَوَابًا وَاذْهَبْ إِلَى جَزَائِرِ الْكَافُورِ وَاخْطُبْ بِنْتَ مَلِكِهَا لِوَلَدِي
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika aḥḍara wazīrahu wa-qāla lahu dabbir lī raʾyan fī amri waladī yakūnu ṣawāban wa-idhhab ilā jazāʾiri al-kāfūri wa-ukhṭub binta malikihā li-waladī
sentences.l: Then the king had his vizier brought and said to him: Contrive for me a plan in the matter of my son (that) will be right; and go to the Islands of the Camphor and ask-in-marriage the daughter of its king for my son.
sentences.i: Then the king summoned his vizier and said to him, “Work out a sound plan for me in my son’s affair: go to the Camphor Islands and ask the hand of their king’s daughter for my son.”
sentences.n: The print has وزبره, a misprint for وزيره (wazīrahu, “his vizier”), corrected here. dabbir lī raʾyan, “contrive for me a plan”. bint malikihā, “the daughter of its king”: the -hā refers to the islands taken together. li-waladī, li- “for”: on behalf of my son.

sentences.t: فَأَجَابَهُ الْوَزِيرُ بِالسَّمْعِ وَالطَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ajābahu al-wazīru bi-al-samʿi wa-al-ṭāʿati
sentences.l: So the vizier answered him with the hearing and the obedience.
sentences.i: The vizier answered him with hearing and obedience.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ عَادَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ إِلَى مَنْزِلِهِ وَقَدْ زَادَ بِهِ الْوَجْدُ وَالْحَالُ وَطَالَ عَلَيْهِ الْمِطَالُ
sentences.tr: thumma ʿāda tāju al-mulūki ilā manzilihi wa-qad zāda bihi al-wajdu wa-al-ḥālu wa-ṭāla ʿalayhi al-miṭālu
sentences.l: Then Tāj al-Mulūk returned to his dwelling, and the passion and the state had increased with him, and the putting-off grew-long upon him.
sentences.i: Then Tāj al-Mulūk went back to his rooms, his passion and his transport grown stronger, and the waiting long and heavy upon him.
sentences.n: zāda bihi, “increased with him”, grew upon him. al-ḥāl, “the state”: here the overwhelmed state of the lover, the word the mystics use for a rapture that comes over one. al-miṭāl, “putting off”, the verbal noun of māṭala, to delay: the waiting seemed long to him. ḥāl and miṭāl rhyme.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّيْلُ بَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā janna ʿalayhi al-laylu bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā wa-anshada yaqūlu shiʿrun
sentences.l: And when the night darkened upon him, he wept and moaned and complained, and recited, saying: Verse:
sentences.i: When night closed over him, he wept and moaned and lamented, and recited these lines:
sentences.n: janna ʿalayhi al-layl, “night darkened over him”, the verb of covering and hiding. anna, “he moaned”, from anīn, moaning. bakā and ishtakā rhyme. shiʿr, “verse”, is the print’s heading for the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
جَنَّ الظَّلَامُ وَدَمْعِي زَائِدُ الْمَدَدِ * وَالْوَجْدُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ النِّيْرَانِ فِيْ كَبِدِيْ
سَلُوا اللَّيَالِي عَنِّي وَهْيَ تُخْبِرُكُمْ * اِنْ كَانَ شُغْلِي غَيْرَ الْهَمِّ وَالْكَمَدِ
اَبِيتُ اَرْعَى نُجُومَ اللَّيْلِ مِنْ وَلَهِي * وَالدَّمْعُ مُنْهَمِلٌ فِي الْخَدِّ كَالْبَرَدِ
وَقَدْ بَقِيتُ وَحِيدًا لَيْسَ لِي اَحَدٌ * كَمِثْلِ صَبٍّ بِلَا اَهْلٍ وَلَا وَلَدِ
sentences.tr:
janna al-ẓalāmu wa-damʿī zāʾidu al-madadi * wa-al-wajdu min shiddati al-nīrāni fī kabidī
salū al-layāliya ʿannī wa-hya tukhbirukum * in kāna shughlī ghayra al-hammi wa-al-kamadi
abītu arʿā nujūma al-layli min walahī * wa-al-damʿu munhamilun fī al-khaddi ka-al-baradi
wa-qad baqītu waḥīdan laysa lī aḥadun * ka-mithli ṣabbin bi-lā ahlin wa-lā waladi
sentences.l:
The darkness has fallen, and my tears (are) increasing of supply, * and the passion, from the fierceness of the fires, (is) in my liver.
Ask the nights about me, and they will tell you * whether my occupation was other than the care and the grief.
I pass-the-night tending the stars of the night out of my love-madness, * and the tear (is) pouring on the cheek like the hail.
And I have remained alone, there is not to me anyone, * like-the-like of a love-sick-one without family and without child.
sentences.i:
Darkness has fallen, and my tears flow ever more; * the fierce fire of passion burns within my liver.
Ask the nights about me, and they will tell you * whether I have had any task but care and grief.
I spend the night watching the stars, distraught with love, * the tears pouring down my cheek like hail.
And I am left alone, with no one of my own, * like a lovesick man with neither kin nor child.
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. The liver, kabid, is the seat of grief and passion in Arabic poetry, where English would say the heart. wa-hya, “and they”, with the hāʾ shortened, as verse allows. in kāna, “whether”. raʿā al-nujūm, “to tend the stars” as a herdsman tends a flock, is the sleepless lover’s watch. ka-mithli, “like the like of”, a doubled comparison common in verse; a ṣabb is a lover sick with longing.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ لَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ غُشِيَ عَلَيْهِ سَاعَةً فَلَمْ يُفِقْ إِلَّا وَقْتَ الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: thumma lammā faragha min shiʿrihi ghushiya ʿalayhi sāʿatan fa-lam yufiq illā waqta al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: Then when he finished from his verse, he was-fainted for an hour, and he did not come-to except (at) the time of the morning.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses he fell into a faint, and did not come to himself until morning.
sentences.n: ghushiya ʿalayhi, “(a covering) came over him”, the usual impersonal passive for fainting. sāʿatan, “an hour”, a while: the while lasted till dawn. afāqa, “to come to, recover”.

sentences.t: فَأَتَى خَادِمُ أَبِيهِ وَوَقَفَ عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ وَدَعَاهُ إِلَى وَالِدِهِ فَرَاحَ مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-atā khādimu abīhi wa-waqafa ʿinda raʾsihi wa-daʿāhu ilā wālidihi fa-rāḥa maʿahu
sentences.l: So the servant of his father came and stood at his head and called him to his father, so he went with him.
sentences.i: Then his father’s servant came and stood at his head and summoned him to his father, and he went with him.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهُ أَبُوهُ وَجَدَهُ قَدْ تَغَيَّرَ لَوْنُهُ فَصَبَّرَهُ وَوَعَدَهُ بِجَمْعِ شَمْلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu abūhu wajadahu qad taghayyara lawnuhu fa-ṣabbarahu wa-waʿadahu bi-jamʿi shamlihi
sentences.l: So when his father saw him, he found him (that) his colour had changed; so he made-him-patient and promised him the gathering of his scattered-state.
sentences.i: When his father saw him, he found that his colour had changed; he bade him be patient and promised him that he would be united with his beloved.
sentences.n: ṣabbarahu, “he made him patient”: he comforted him and told him to hold on. waʿadahu bi-, “promised him”: what is promised takes bi-. jamʿ shamlihi, “the gathering of his scattered state”: shaml is what holds a man’s affairs, or two lovers, together, and to “gather the shaml” is to reunite them.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَهَّزَ عَزِيزًا مَعَ وَزِيرِهِ وَأَعْطَاهُمُ الْهَدَايَا فَسَافَرُوا أَيَّامًا وَلَيَالِيَ إِلَى أَنْ أَشْرَفُوا عَلَى جَزَائِرِ الْكَافُورِ
sentences.tr: thumma jahhaza ʿazīzan maʿa wazīrihi wa-aʿṭāhumu al-hadāyā fa-sāfarū ayyāman wa-layāliya ilā an ashrafū ʿalā jazāʾiri al-kāfūri
sentences.l: Then he equipped ʿAzīz with his vizier and gave them the gifts; so they travelled days and nights until they looked-down upon the Islands of the Camphor.
sentences.i: Then he fitted out ʿAzīz to go with his vizier and gave them the gifts, and they travelled for days and nights until they came within sight of the Camphor Islands.
sentences.n: jahhaza, “to equip, fit out” for a journey. al-hadāyā, “the gifts” a suitor’s embassy carries. ashrafa ʿalā, “to overlook”, to come within sight of a place from a height.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ أَقَامُوا عَلَى شَاطِئِ نَهْرٍ وَأَنْفَذَ الْوَزِيرُ رَسُولًا مِنْ عِنْدِهِ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ لِيُخْبِرَهُ بِقُدُومِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika aqāmū ʿalā shāṭiʾi nahrin wa-anfadha al-wazīru rasūlan min ʿindihi ilā al-maliki li-yukhbirahu bi-qudūmihim
sentences.l: So at that they stayed on the bank of a river, and the vizier dispatched a messenger from with him to the king to inform him of their arrival.
sentences.i: There they halted on the bank of a river, and the vizier sent a messenger of his own on to the king to tell him they had come.
sentences.n: anfadha, “to send off, dispatch”. min ʿindihi, “from his side”, one of his own people. li-yukhbirahu bi-qudūmihim, “so that he might tell him of their arrival”: li- “so that”, and akhbara takes the news with bi-.

sentences.t: فَرَاحَ الرَّسُولُ فَلَمْ يَكُنْ غَيْرَ سَاعَةٍ إِلَّا وَحُجَّابُ الْمَلِكِ وَأُمَرَاؤُهُ قَدْ أَقْبَلُوا عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَاقَوْهُمْ مِنْ مَسِيرَةِ فَرْسَخٍ فَتَلَقَّوْهُمْ وَسَارُوا فِي خِدْمَتِهِمْ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلُوا بِهِمْ عَلَى الْمَلِكِ فَقَدَّمُوا لَهُ الْهَدَايَا وَأَقَامُوا فِي ضِيَافَتِهِ ثَلٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: fa-rāḥa al-rasūlu fa-lam yakun ghayra sāʿatin illā wa-ḥujjābu al-maliki wa-umarāʾuhu qad aqbalū ʿalayhim wa-lāqawhum min masīrati farsakhin fa-talaqqawhum wa-sārū fī khidmatihim ilā an dakhalū bihim ʿalā al-maliki fa-qaddamū lahu al-hadāyā wa-aqāmū fī ḍiyāfatihi thalāthata ayyāmin
sentences.l: So the messenger went; and it was not other than an hour but the chamberlains of the king and his emirs had come-forward to them and met them from the going of a parasang; so they received them and went in their service until they entered with them before the king; so they presented to him the gifts and stayed in his hospitality three days.
sentences.i: The messenger went, and within the hour the king’s chamberlains and emirs were riding out towards them; they came a parasang’s distance to meet them, received them, and escorted them with all attention until they brought them in before the king. They presented the gifts to him, and stayed three days as his guests.
sentences.n: fa-lam yakun ghayra sāʿatin illā wa-, “it was no more than an hour before …”: a spoken pattern, with illā wa- bringing in what happened. farsakh, “parasang”, a Persian measure of distance, about three miles; masīrat farsakh, “a parasang’s going”. dakhalū bihim ʿalā al-malik, “they went in with them to the king”: dakhala bi- is to bring someone in. The print itself sets a dagger alif in ثلٰثة.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَ الْيَوْمُ الرَّابِعُ قَامَ الْوَزِيرُ وَدَخَلَ عَلَى الْمَلِكِ وَوَقَفَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَحَدَّثَهُ بِالْأَمْرِ الَّذِي جَاءَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kāna al-yawmu al-rābiʿu qāma al-wazīru wa-dakhala ʿalā al-maliki wa-waqafa bayna yadayhi wa-ḥaddathahu bi-al-amri alladhī jāʾa fīhi
sentences.l: So when it was the day the fourth, the vizier rose and went-in to the king and stood between his hands and told him of the matter which he had come in.
sentences.i: On the fourth day the vizier rose, went in to the king, stood before him, and told him the business on which he had come.
sentences.n: bayna yadayhi, “between his hands”, in his presence. ḥaddathahu bi-, “told him of”: bi- marks what is told. jāʾa fīhi, “came in it”, came about it.

sentences.t: فَبَقِيَ الْمَلِكُ حَائِرًا فِي رَدِّ الْجَوَابِ لِأَنَّ ابْنَتَهُ لَاتُحِبُّ الرِّجَالَ وَلَا تَشْتَهِى الزَّوَاجَ
sentences.tr: fa-baqiya al-maliku ḥāʾiran fī raddi al-jawābi li-anna ibnatahu lā tuḥibbu al-rijāla wa-lā tashtahī al-zawāja
sentences.l: So the king remained perplexed in the returning of the answer, because his daughter does not love the men and does not desire the marriage.
sentences.i: The king was at a loss how to answer, for his daughter had no love for men and no wish to marry.
sentences.n: radd al-jawāb, “returning the answer”, giving a reply. The present tense, “does not love”, stands because it is still true. The print runs lā and tuḥibbu together (لاتحب) and writes the final yāʾ of tashtahī without its dots (تشتهى); both are kept.

sentences.t: فَأَطْرَقَ الْمَلِكُ بِرَأْسِهِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ سَاعَةً ثُمَّ رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ وَدَعَا بِخَادِمٍ مِنْ بَعْضِ الْخُدَّامِ وَقَالَ لَهُ اذْهَبْ إِلَى سَيِّدَتِكَ دُنْيَا وَأَعِدْ عَلَيْهَا مَا سَمِعْتَ وَبِمَا جَاءَبِهِ هَذَا الْوَزِيرُ
sentences.tr: fa-aṭraqa al-maliku bi-raʾsihi ilā al-arḍi sāʿatan thumma rafaʿa raʾsahu wa-daʿā bi-khādimin min baʿḍi al-khuddāmi wa-qāla lahu idhhab ilā sayyidatika dunyā wa-aʿid ʿalayhā mā samiʿta wa-bi-mā jāʾa bihi hādhā al-wazīru
sentences.l: So the king lowered with his head to the ground an hour, then raised his head and called for a servant from some of the servants and said to him: Go to your mistress Dunyā and repeat to her what you heard, and of what this vizier has come with.
sentences.i: The king bowed his head towards the ground for a while; then he raised it, called for one of his servants, and said to him, “Go to your mistress Dunyā and repeat to her what you have heard, and what this vizier has come with.”
sentences.n: The print has جأبه, a misprint for جاءبه (jāʾa bihi, “he came with”), corrected here; the two words stay run together as printed. aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi, “he lowered his head”, the gesture of a man thinking; bi- marks the head as what he bowed. daʿā bi-, “called for”. aʿid ʿalayhā, “repeat to her”. wa-bi-mā jāʾa bihi, “and of what he came with”: the first bi- hangs loosely on an understood “tell her”; jāʾa bi- is to bring.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الْخَادِمُ وَذَهَبَ وَغَابَ سَاعَةً ثُمَّ عَادَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَامَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ إِنِّي لَمَّا دَخَلْتُ وَأَخْبَرْتُ السِّتَّ دُنْيَا بِمَا سَمِعْتُ غَضِبَتْ غَضَبًا شَدِيدًا وَنَهَضَتْ إِلَيَّ بِعَصَاةٍ وَأَرَادَتْ كَسْرَ رَأْسِي فَفَرَرْتُ مِنْهَا هَارِبًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-khādimu wa-dhahaba wa-ghāba sāʿatan thumma ʿāda ilā al-maliki wa-qāla lahu yā malika al-zamāni innī lammā dakhaltu wa-akhbartu al-sitta dunyā bi-mā samiʿtu ghaḍibat ghaḍaban shadīdan wa-nahaḍat ilayya bi-ʿaṣātin wa-arādat kasra raʾsī fa-farartu minhā hāriban
sentences.l: So the servant rose and went and was-absent an hour, then returned to the king and said to him: O king of the age, I — when I entered and informed the Lady Dunyā of what I heard, she became-angry a severe anger and rose against me with a stick and wanted the breaking of my head; so I fled from her, running-away.
sentences.i: The servant rose and went, and was gone a while; then he came back to the king and said to him, “King of the age, when I went in and told the lady Dunyā what I had heard, she flew into a violent rage, came at me with a stick, and meant to break my head; and I ran from her.
sentences.n: al-sitt, “the lady”, the spoken word for a mistress of the house. innī lammā dakhaltu … ghaḍibat, “I, when I went in … she grew angry”: the sentence begins with the servant and ends with her. ghaḍibat ghaḍaban shadīdan, “she was angry with a fierce anger”: the verbal noun repeats the verb for force. The print spells the stick ʿaṣā with a final tāʾ marbūṭa (عصاة); the sense is plain, and it is kept as printed. The print runs yā and malik together (ياملك); kept.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِي إِنْ كَانَ أَبِى يَغْصِبُنِى عَلَى الزَّوَاجِ فَالَّذِي أَتَزَوَّجُ بِهِ أَقْتُلُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lī in kāna abī yaghṣibunī ʿalā al-zawāji fa-alladhī atazawwaju bihi aqtuluhu
sentences.l: And she said to me: If my father is forcing me to the marriage, then the-one whom I am married with, I will kill him.
sentences.i: And she said to me, ‘If my father forces me to marry, I will kill the man I am married to.’”
sentences.n: ghaṣabahu ʿalā, “to force (someone) into”. alladhī atazawwaju bihi aqtuluhu, “the one I marry, I will kill him”: the object is set at the head of the sentence and taken up again by -hu. atazawwaju bihi, “I am married with him”: tazawwaja takes its partner with bi- as well as directly. The final yāʾ of abī and yaghṣibunī is printed without its dots (ى); kept.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَبُوهَا لِلْوَزِيرِ وَلِعَزِيزٍ قَدْ سَمِعْتُمَا فَأَنْتُمَا تَعْلَمَانِ وَأَخْبِرَا الْمَلِكَ بِذَلِكَ وَسَلِّمَا وَأَنَّ ابْنَتِي لَاتُحِبُّ الرِّجَالَ وَلَا تَشْتَهِى الزَّوَاجَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla abūhā li-al-wazīri wa-li-ʿazīzin qad samiʿtumā fa-antumā taʿlamāni wa-akhbirā al-malika bi-dhālika wa-sallimā wa-anna ibnatī lā tuḥibbu al-rijāla wa-lā tashtahī al-zawāja
sentences.l: So her father said to the vizier and to ʿAzīz: You-two have heard, so you-two know; and inform the king of that, and give-greeting, and that my daughter does not love the men and does not desire the marriage.
sentences.i: Then her father said to the vizier and to ʿAzīz, “You have both heard it, so now you know. Tell your king of this, give him my greetings, and tell him that my daughter has no love for men and no wish to marry.”
sentences.n: The print has ولعزير, a misprint for ولعزيز (wa-li-ʿAzīz, “and to ʿAzīz”), corrected here: the last letter has lost its dot. The duals -tumā, -ā speak to the two envoys together. akhbirā … bi-dhālika, “tell (him) of that”: akhbara takes the news with bi-. sallimā, “give greeting”, take my salutation to the king. wa-anna ibnatī, “and that my daughter”: the anna hangs loosely on akhbirā. The print again runs lā and tuḥibbu together and writes tashtahī with an undotted final yāʾ; kept.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
sentences.n: The print sets the name in two words here, شهر زاد; kept.
